elements.text: The pattern for all three is similar. server derives from node, but neither derive from network. node and server establish base functionality for the applicable context, and then multiply-derive network to mix in the core network functionality. Overall there is very little duplication, although network::session_server and network::session_inbound are very similar. These could probably be collapsed, but I've specifically avoided crossing the peer-to-peer and client-server streams above the lowest level base classes.

text:
I completed the electrum `handle_blockchain_block_header()` and `handle_blockchain_block_headers()` methods. This was a little more than  expected because version 1.4 added a checkpointing scheme designed to minimize *header* download at clients. Headers are small, and this feature introduces additional trust beyond SPV (trust of header checkpoints embedded in the wallet code).

Implementing this requires computing a unique merkle tree of *all block hashes* up to the given block - for any block on demand. This  requires caching partial merkle root computations at fixed intervals across the full chain. The caching is fast and very small, and the query computations are reasonable. But it was a lot of moving parts to organize and test.

It is controllable via config, and we'd want it off unless supporting electrum. A large depth effectively precludes the cache, since it's cached on block height intervals of `2^depth`. The cache is associated to blocks vs. heights (reorg safe) and append-only in the `txs` table. This should set to `11` (caching one merkle subtree root hash for every `2048` blocks) when serving electrum. Otherwise checkpointed header queries produce a merkle tree spanning the entire header chain (`O(n)` where n is the number of blocks) and will take some time.
```[database]
interval_depth = 255```

elements.text: The cache simply slips into the txs association table record for every interval block. This is simple because txs is a slab table (variably-sized records). This can also be done as blocks are concurrently downloaded and stored out of order, since the computed interval merkle root is a function of header hashes within an interval, set at the last block of each interval. So it's not necessary that preceding blocks be downloaded (header chain is already archived).

elements.text: Given that the interval is controlled by a one byte config value, which if changed after some amount of sync will cause a catastrophic store failure, I'm going to set that one byte as the first value in the genesis block txs entry. This will be read at startup and cause the config value to be ignored after store creation (which stores the genesis block).

elements.text: A huddle started

I split the application logic from the fee querying, so that the database code for the fee estimation is now independent (just fee collection) and about 100 lines. That's parallelized over blocks, and can be radically optimized within each block (and for individual block queries, parallelized by tx).

The application logic becomes a server class, initialized and updated using a vector of fee  vectors (blocks -> txs -> fees). This allows for parallel fee collection by block, which is optimal for the initialization. The cache is then just member state of the class.

The factoring makes testing significantly easier and simplifies the logic. Small impact on performance by prob not even noticeable. This is because the population query is parallel but the computation is independent. The computation can be made parallel as well, but setting it up twice is additional overhead, and may not even be worth it.

I've left the atomics in so I can compare it. But with sequential computation the atomics can be dropped. That is a bit simplifying, and a also enables dynamic sizing for the buckets if we wanted to do that. I also verified that the Core implementation is fixed buckets.

Also updated the logic to allow for < 1 sat per byte fee rate, which was easy. Unlike Core, we don't rely on a populated vector to tell us the bucket values, since that's just nanosecond math. Not worth the additional complexity and giant lookup table. Also we don't operate in a multiple of 1000 (sats per 1000 bytes) because it's all floating point to start with, and there's ridiculous precision in a double. So we just compute in sat per vbyte, and set the min/max at compile (presently). To emit in per kvb units (e.g. for compat APIs, we obviously just divide it out).

elements.text: Saved a couple MB (variably-sized records) by removing fees from the validate_bk table and converting it to an array. Given that it doesn't get populated unless fully validating or populating block filters, it wasn't consistently available anyway. Since block fees are not required by either validation or candidate block creation, and they can be queried quickly enough for service query and service fee estimator initialization, there's no reason for the cache.

elements.text: I've used some of the above space by adding a non-witness size (for blocks) to the txs table. This is 32 bits per block and sits next to the witness size. This matches the pair of values in the tx table. That allows us to produce virtual byte size for blocks and txs at almost no cost, which optimizes for fee computation. The two sizes in the txs table could be compressed using variable sized integer, which would cut the storage way down. Also we can compress the is_coinbase bit in the tx table into one of the sizes, which would eliminate 1byte per tx, or around 1GB total.

elements.text: I see that in the release notes for BC 31 they have added spender indexing. This is integral to BS, and I assume they are trying to close these gaps where possible. This will give us a more comparable store size metric, since this is a large index - especially if you also store whole blocks independently as BC does. With this and tx indexing enabled and with our address index disabled, the indexation is fairly comparable. Yet we are about the same size without it, which means this should highlight the space inefficiency of storing whole blocks. IIRC client filters are optional for BC (as for BS).

elements.text:
I've completed the direct block/tx fee query optimization.  Not only does this significantly optimize the fee accumulator initialization and updates, but also gets us very close to full optimization for all of our REST queries. There were a few that required population of the full block or tx from the store, as well as previous outputs, in order to obtain computed properties (such as fees).

This is now reduced to just the
sigops

property. Sigops can be computed directly via query, just like I've done with fees. I'll probably do that eventually, at least when we get to candidate block generations. sigops and fees were originally intended for caching, but the requirement for prevouts precludes caching during archival, and to preserve the performance of milestone sync, we don't want to compel validation queries just for this. Since these cached values are not used in validation, the query performance is more than sufficient. In the mean time I may drop the sigops field from the native REST queries in order to get the performance benefit of avoiding the full block/tx queries just for this one property.

elements.text: I've dropped sigops and wtxid from native interface for now. These block/tx details methods will no longer populate the full tx or block objects and so are very fast, but these two values would still require that full object population. The perf boost is a side benefit of yesterday's work to optimize fee and fee rate queries for the electrum and bitcoind fee estimation methods. I'll be hooking up the fee estimator in server today, and integrating it into the several dependent service methods.

elements.text:
Not only are the fee computations now direct relational queries, but for blocks they are executed concurrently by tx. Because spend and value are both output in the API, this results in two independent calls to summarize inputs and outputs, both summing concurrently over txs in the block.

For a single query to just obtain the fees for each tx, or for the block as a whole, this is further optimized to operating in a single concurrent run over all txs. That's not used above but is used to initialize the fee estimation accumulator, which by default collects fee data for all txs in the top 10,000 blocks. I expect this to now be sufficiently fast to allow it to initialize from the store at each server startup (when enabled), so there will be no need to cache fee accumulator state (e.g. as BC does). If each block takes 1ms then a 1000 block fee accumulator will be initialized just 1sec after startup. For a cold stare this will take a little longer, but should still be sufficiently fast. And there's no need to block startup for this, it can just give service callers a busy response until ready.

elements.text: Above should read 1,000 blocks in both instances (not 10,000). Technically it's 1,008, based on the maximum horizon value. This is chosen arbitrarily to target 1 week of blocks.

Caching to disk not only adds complexity, in this case it expires quickly anyway. We try to derive everything possible from store state to avoid these various sidecars. I should have a cache initialization time cost soon.
